scenes: A rule is triggered by a fact, and it reads only facts.
So it is exact.
It may do anything you wrote in it.
Here a fake secret that no honest task uses is about to leave the computer.
The rule denies it, stops the computer and alerts you.
A precaution is triggered by a report or an opinion, and those can be wrong.
An opinion: a classifier thinks an agent is working against you.
Or a report: an agent program's own account does not match what Silo saw.
Because its trigger can be wrong, a precaution takes only reversible actions, such as alert, checkpoint, pause, deny and hold.
It never allows, never resumes and never stops a computer.
Silo is built so that such a precaution cannot even be written.
Like a rule, a precaution is kept outside the computer, and nothing inside can change it.
What an agent may see of it is still open.
Who or what triggers something decides what it may do.
You can do anything.
A fact, through a rule, does what the rule says.
A report or an opinion, through a precaution, does only what can be undone.
A budget shows the difference.
On a computer it is a rule: the boundary counts every call.
On a run it is a precaution: which run made a call is an opinion.
A wrong grant lets something out that cannot be taken back.
A wrong pause costs time.
A classifier itself never acts.
And there is no detour.
That a classifier gave an opinion, or that a precaution acted, is itself a fact.
No rule may be triggered by it.
A rule or a precaution can be synchronous or asynchronous.
Synchronous: the thing waits at the boundary for the answer, so it can still be denied or held.
A rule answers on the spot, because a fact is known on the spot.
Here the budget of main is reached, and in this example the next model call is denied.
A precaution makes the thing wait for a classifier's opinion.
Here the opinion is not safe, and the precaution denies it.
Asynchronous: nothing waits, and only the computer is left to act on.
A rule: the memory of the Mac runs low.
The meter is a fact, and in this example the rule pauses main and alerts you.
A precaution: a classifier's opinion comes after the thing has passed, and the precaution pauses main.
The timing does not change the kinds: a rule may trigger any kind, and a precaution only reversible ones.
A model's reply asks for a command to be run: a tool call.
It waits at the boundary for a classifier.
That wait has a limit too, and Silo ends it itself.
If the opinion is safe, the precaution does nothing, and the call passes as the rules allow.
If it is unsure, in this example the precaution holds it for you.
Here it says: not safe.
The precaution denies the call, and Silo changes the reply: the tool call is replaced by a refusal.
The agent program sends the refusal back with its next request, and the model reads it.
The original and the replacement are both kept as facts.
This works where Silo can read the model's traffic.
How each agent program takes a changed reply is still to be tested.
A classifier can be fooled: a bad action can be cut into steps that each look innocent.
A rule at the boundary cannot be got around, even by an agent that knows it by heart.
So the rules are the promise, and a precaution is extra caution on top.
